scenes.say: Anyone can type any email. How does your server know who's calling? By the end you'll store passwords, read a token, and stop one client flooding your API.

lines.text: Then: how much may they call?

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Store passwords and read a token. Log in with Google safely. And stop one client flooding your API.
lines: Stop one client flooding your API

scenes.title: How do we store passwords?
scenes.statement: If the database leaks, no password may leak with it.

example.output: a stored value nobody can reverse

scenes.say: Users sign up with passwords like hunter two, and the database may leak one day. We want to store something nobody can turn back into the password.

scenes.head: A hash is a meat grinder
scenes.say: Start with passwords. Never store them. Think of beef, a meat grinder, and mince. Nobody turns mince back into beef. A hash works the same: no way back. At login, grind what they typed, and compare.

scenes.head: Sign up, then log in
scenes.say: Sign up. We feed hunter two to b crypt. Out comes one string, with four parts. Algorithm, b crypt. Cost twelve, meaning two to the twelfth rounds. A random salt: random bytes mixed into the password, fresh for every user. So a precomputed table of common hashes is useless. And the hash itself. At login, we take the salt from that string, hash the typed password again, and compare. Same hash: match.

scenes.head: bcrypt in Python
scenes.say: In Python. Hash the same password twice, each with a fresh salt. Print the first seven characters: algorithm and cost. The two hashes differ, yet check password says true. The salt follows, inside the same string.

panels.code:
import bcrypt
pw = b"hunter2"
h1 = bcrypt.hashpw(pw, bcrypt.gensalt(12))
h2 = bcrypt.hashpw(pw, bcrypt.gensalt(12))
print(h1.decode()[:7])
print(h1 != h2, bcrypt.checkpw(pw, h1))

scenes.say: Your turn. Alice and Bob both pick the password hunter two. Does the users table store the same hash for both? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Alice and Bob both pick `hunter2`. Same stored hash?

scenes.head: Three ways to store a password
scenes.say: No. Each user gets a fresh salt, so the hashes differ. Plain text leaks everything the moment the database leaks. A plain fast hash lets attackers guess billions a second on a graphics card. B crypt is slow on purpose. Argon two is a modern alternative.
rows: slow on purpose, unique per user

scenes.say: That answers our problem. A slow salted hash means a leak reveals no passwords.

scenes.title: How does the server know it's you?
scenes.statement: Every request must prove who is calling, without the password.

example.input: a request carrying a cookie or token

scenes.say: You're logged in. Now every request must prove who is calling, like this one with a cookie. We want the server to know it is user forty two.

scenes.head: A coat check ticket
scenes.say: Every request must prove who you are. Think of a coat check. You hand in your coat: that's logging in. You get a ticket: a session id, in a cookie. Each visit, you show the ticket. The clerk fetches your coat: the server finds user forty two.

scenes.head: A session lookup
scenes.say: Request one: the browser sends cookie abc nine. The server asks the session store: who is abc nine? The store answers, user forty two. Now the server knows who's calling. To log out, the server deletes the row. The ticket stops working at once.

scenes.head: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is readable
scenes.say: Now the other way. A J W T needs no store. It has three parts joined by dots: header, payload, signature. Here's one for user forty two. Anyone can decode the payload. It prints sub forty two and an expiry.

panels.code:
import jwt, json, base64
KEY = "a-long-secret-key-of-32-bytes-min!"
claims = {"sub": "42", "exp": 1893456000}
tok = jwt.encode(claims, KEY, "HS256")
head, body, sig = tok.split(".")
raw = base64.urlsafe_b64decode(body + "==")
print(json.loads(raw))

scenes.head: Readable, but not editable
scenes.say: So can a user edit it? Change sub from forty two to one, keep the old signature, and verify. Rejected: the signature no longer matches. Signed, not secret.

panels.code:
import jwt, base64
KEY = "a-long-secret-key-of-32-bytes-min!"
head, _, sig = jwt.encode({"sub": "42"}, KEY, "HS256").split(".")
b64 = lambda s: base64.urlsafe_b64encode(s.encode()).decode().rstrip("=")
forged = head + "." + b64('{"sub": "1"}') + "." + sig
try:
    jwt.decode(forged, KEY, ["HS256"])
except jwt.InvalidTokenError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e)

scenes.say: Your turn. The token lasts an hour. The user logs out at minute five. A thief copied the token. At minute ten, does it work? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: JWT valid 1 hour. Logout at minute 5. Copied token at minute 10?

scenes.head: Session vs JWT
scenes.say: Still accepted. Valid signature, expiry not reached, no list on the server. Where state lives: sessions keep it on the server, JWTs in the token. Logout: a session dies instantly. A JWT lives until it expires. Scaling: sessions need a shared store. Any server can verify a JWT. Size: a cookie is tiny, a JWT is bigger.
rows: on the server: id to user

scenes.head: Where does the token live?
scenes.say: Where does the browser keep it? Not in local storage: a script an attacker injects into your page can read it. Use an HttpOnly, Secure cookie: scripts can't read it. And never put secrets in a JWT. Anyone can decode it.
rows: any injected script can read it
scripts can't read it; HTTPS only

scenes.say: So the server knows. A session id or a signed token tells it who is calling.

scenes.title: How do we log in with Google?
scenes.statement: Let people sign in with Google while the app never sees their Google password.

example.output: the app learns who you are, nothing more

scenes.say: Next problem. Sign in with Google, but our app never sees the password. For example, one click on log in with Google. We want the app to learn who you are, nothing more.

scenes.head: A valet key
scenes.say: The app wants to know who you are, not your Google password. That's OAuth, short for Open Authorization. Think of a valet key. It starts the car but can't open the trunk. OAuth gives the app a limited key, never the master key.

scenes.head: OAuth in four arrows
scenes.say: Here's the dance. One: the app redirects you to Google. Two: you log in at Google and approve. Three: Google sends you back with a short lived code. Four: the app's server swaps the code for a token, using a secret only it knows. Your password never left Google.
Your turn. The code travels through the browser's address bar. A thief copies it. Is the code alone enough to get your token? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: A thief copies the short lived code. Enough to get the token?

scenes.head: A stolen code is not enough
scenes.say: No. The swap needs the app's secret, and only the app's server has it. The thief arrives with a code and no secret, and Google says no. That's why the code goes through the browser, but the token never does.

scenes.head: Authn vs authz
scenes.say: OAuth tells the app who you are. That is authentication: failing it is four oh one. What you may do is a separate check, authorization. Failing that is four oh three.
Problem solved. OAuth shows the app who you are, without your password.

scenes.title: How do we stop one client flooding?
scenes.statement: Limit how much one user may call: bursts are fine, floods are not.
scenes.say: Now, how much may they call? Say user forty two fires fifteen requests at once. We want ten to pass, and five to get four twenty nine.

scenes.head: From who to how much
scenes.say: The key is user forty two, from the token. Picture an arcade coin jar. Each game costs one coin. The jar refills one coin a second, never above ten.

scenes.head: Fifteen requests, ten coins
scenes.say: The token says sub forty two, so that's the key: one bucket per user. User forty two sends a burst of fifteen requests at the same instant. Each takes a coin. Ten coins, ten requests pass. The last five are rejected with four twenty nine.

scenes.head: The whole algorithm
scenes.say: The code needs no timer. We store the coins, and the time of the last request. Each request, compute what was earned. Cap it at capacity. At least one? Spend it and say yes. Otherwise no. Constant time, constant memory per user.

scenes.head: Fifteen at once
scenes.say: Now run it. Capacity ten, one coin a second. Fifteen requests at the same instant. Count the passes. Ten pass, five fail. One second later, a coin is back. In real code, now comes from the clock.

panels.code:
b = TokenBucket(rate=1, cap=10)
passed = 0
for i in range(15):
    if b.allow(0): passed += 1
print(passed, 15 - passed)
print(b.allow(1))

scenes.say: Your turn. The bucket is empty after the burst. Three seconds pass. Five more requests arrive together. How many pass? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Empty bucket, +1 per second. 3 s later, 5 requests arrive. Passes?

scenes.head: Five requests, three seconds later
scenes.say: Three. Three seconds earned three coins. Refill sets the long run speed. Of five requests, three pass and two get four twenty nine.
There's our answer. A bucket per user lets ten through and rejects five.

scenes.title: One limit across many servers
scenes.statement: Two servers each count requests. How do we enforce one limit for the user across both?
scenes.say: Last problem. Two servers each count requests. For example, a limit of ten, and twenty requests split across them. We want only ten to pass in total.
Your turn. Two servers, each with its own local bucket of ten. One client sends ten requests to each. How many pass? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 2 servers, local bucket of 10 each. 10 requests to each. Pass?

scenes.head: Local buckets leak
scenes.say: Twenty. Each server sees ten requests and its own full bucket, so everything passes. The limit was ten. The client got twenty.

scenes.head: One shared bucket, one step
scenes.say: The fix is one shared bucket in Redis, a fast shared store, with a key per user. Both servers ask Redis. But one coin is left. Both servers read one, and both spend it. Two pass. So the read and the spend must be atomic. Atomic means no request slips in between. A small Lua script, a tiny program that runs inside Redis, does it.

scenes.head: Three algorithms, one catch each
scenes.say: Token bucket isn't the only limiter. A fixed window counts per minute. A client can spend ten at second fifty nine, ten more at sixty: twenty in two seconds. A sliding window counts the last sixty seconds, at a memory cost. Token bucket allows bursts up to capacity, then holds the average.

scenes.head: What the client sees
scenes.say: Reject with four twenty nine. Add a Retry After header, so clients know when to come back. Classic mistakes: local counters, and two servers spending one token. Capacity sets the burst. Refill sets the average.
rows: local counters; 2 servers read 1, both spend

scenes.say: And that's one limit across servers. One shared Redis bucket, updated atomically, enforces it.

scenes.head: Sessions or JWT?
scenes.say: Sessions or J W T? A session lives on the server: instant logout, but servers need a shared store. Any server verifies a J W T, but you can't revoke it early. Where's the token kept? In an HttpOnly cookie, so scripts can't read it.
rows: JWT: any server verifies, no revoke till expiry

scenes.head: Passwords and access
scenes.say: How do you store passwords? As a slow salted hash, like b crypt or Argon two. Why not plain S H A? It's fast, so attackers guess billions a second. Authentication is who you are. Failing it gives four oh one. Authorization is what you may do. Failing it gives four oh three.
rows: slow salted hash: bcrypt or Argon2
fast: billions of guesses a second
what you may do; failing it: 403

scenes.head: How does OAuth work?
scenes.say: How does O Auth work? The app redirects you to Google. You log in there and approve. Google sends you back with a short lived code. The app's server swaps it for a token, using its secret. So the app never sees your password.

scenes.head: Build a token bucket
scenes.say: How do you implement a token bucket? Store two numbers per user: coins, and the last request time. Each request adds rate times elapsed seconds, capped at capacity. One coin or more? Spend one and allow it. Otherwise, return four twenty nine. That's O of one.
rows: store coins and last time per user
add rate × elapsed, cap at capacity
one coin or more: spend one, allow

scenes.head: Rate limits in production
scenes.say: Burst versus steady? Capacity sets the burst, refill sets the average. Many servers? One shared bucket in Redis, updated atomically by Lua, tiny code inside Redis. What does the client get? Four twenty nine, with a Retry After header. Common mistake? Local counters, so each server allows the full limit.
rows: shared Redis, atomic Lua, key per user
local counters: each server allows all

scenes.head: Try this tonight
scenes.say: Try three things. Hash the same password twice with bcrypt, and compare the hashes. Decode a token's payload, forge the subject, and watch verification fail. Then write the bucket, and send fifteen requests at once.
So say this. Store passwords as slow salted hashes. A J W T is signed, not secret, and sessions revoke faster. Rate limit with a token bucket per user: capacity is the burst.
lines: Passwords: slow, salted hash. Never store them.
A JWT is signed, not secret. Sessions revoke fast.
One bucket per user: capacity = burst.
